claims.text: Formation of single-phase noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by precursor mobility during nucleation and growth.
Constraining mobility through rapid quenching or limited diffusion time promotes stochastic incorporation of multiple elements.
Constrained mobility produces a uniform, strained single-phase solid solution despite differences in elemental reduction kinetics.
Increased atomic mobility permits thermodynamically driven segregation and phase separation.
The initial material is a mixture containing more than five noble-metal elements targeted for low-temperature formation of uniform, single-phase nanoparticles.
Changing the cooling regime or applying mild annealing can alter atomic diffusion without changing overall composition.
Rapid-heating and rapid-cooling synthesis conditions are regimes in which kinetic factors dominate phase formation.
Limited mobility forces nearly simultaneous incorporation of multiple elements into growing nanoparticles.
Increased mobility allows thermodynamic rearrangement that causes segregation, phase separation, and altered particle morphology.
A more restrictive mobility condition will increase the incidence of single-phase solid solutions, uniform morphology, and lattice strain relative to baseline.
Slower cooling or moderate annealing will increase phase separation, elemental segregation, and morphological heterogeneity relative to baseline.
The baseline rapid-heating and rapid-cooling synthesis stochastically forms single-phase nanoparticles.
Baseline particles exhibit inherent variability, lattice strain, and morphological variation.
The hypothesis applies to systems containing more than five noble metals synthesized from single-source precursor schemes.
The relevant processing boundary occurs when heating and cooling rates are comparable to atomic-diffusion timescales.
The mobility mechanism can be tested by comparing composition-matched mobility-restricted and mobility-enhanced syntheses while holding other parameters constant.
Failure of mobility enhancement to produce a statistically significant increase in phase separation, segregation, or morphological heterogeneity would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The target and stated applicability require more than five elements, but the proposed falsification experiment specifies five-element nanoparticles.
The mediator is defined as mobility during nucleation and growth, whereas one intervention is post-synthesis annealing, which changes mobility after nucleation and growth.
